text: A mineral known as Kryptonite originates from the fictional planet Krypton and becomes radioactive due to the forces that destroyed the planet. This substance, specifically green Kryptonite, is the most commonly recognized form and is responsible for nullifying Superman's powers, causing pain and nausea, and eventually leading to death with prolonged exposure. Kryptonite was introduced in 1943 as a plot device, and while green is the most prevalent, other forms such as red, gold, blue, white, and black have also been introduced, each with distinct effects.
title: Superman

text: Principal photography for *I Am Number Four* started on May 17, 2010, and took place across 20 locations all within the Pittsburgh metropolitan area. DreamWorks chose this region largely because of the Pennsylvania Film Production Tax Credit, and the studio had previously enjoyed a successful shoot of *She's Out of My League* in Pittsburgh in 2008. The production was planned to last between 12 and 13 weeks.
title: I Am Number Four (film)

text: The trunk is a combination of the thoracic, mammary, abdominal, naval, and coxal regions. This region encompasses the central part of the body and is commonly referred to as the torso.
title: List of human anatomical regions

text: The first Christmas card was commissioned by Sir Henry Cole in London on 1st May 1843. Sir Henry Cole also helped introduce the Penny Post three years earlier, which contributed to the success of the card's distribution. The card featured a family raising a toast, with scenes of charity on either side, and was printed in two batches totaling 2,050 cards, each sold for a shilling.
title: Christmas card

text: Defence Against the Dark Arts, often abbreviated as D.A.D.A., is a subject that teaches students how to defend themselves against dark magic and dangerous creatures. Throughout the series, the position has seen a constant turnover, with no teacher remaining in the role for more than one school year. The class is taught by several notable figures, including Quirinus Quirrell, Gilderoy Lockhart, Remus Lupin, Bartemius Crouch Jr. posing as Alastor "Mad-eye" Moody, Dolores Umbridge, Severus Snape, and Amycus Carrow. In the seventh book, Amycus Carrow is specifically named as the teacher of the subject. Hagrid remarks that people have begun to believe the job is cursed, as no one has stayed in the position for long. Dumbledore later suggests that Voldemort placed a curse on the role after his application was rejected, a claim later confirmed by J.K. Rowling. Although Snape was once considered for the position and eventually appointed D.A.D.A. professor in Half-Blood Prince, the role remained unstable until after Voldemort's death, when the curse was lifted and a permanent professor began teaching the subject between the end of Deathly Hallows and the epilogue. Rowling also notes that Harry Potter occasionally gives lectures on the subject.
title: Magic in Harry Potter

text: G. Callen, whose full name is Grisha Alekandrovich Nikolaev, is a fictional character on NCIS: Los Angeles played by Chris O'Donnell. He serves as an NCIS Special Agent in Charge and the senior agent assigned to the Office of Special Projects. The character's first appearance was in the sixth season episode "Legend (Part 1)." Grisha is the full name used to identify the character.
title: G. Callen

text: CLS Group, a specialist US financial institution, offers settlement services to its members in the foreign exchange market (FX). While the forex market operates without a central exchange or clearing facility, businesses using CLS to settle their FX transactions can reduce the settlement risk linked to their trades.
title: CLS Group

text: The German passenger airship LZ 129 Hindenburg was scheduled to fly to Naval Air Station Lakehurst in Manchester Township, New Jersey, United States. Of the 97 people on board (36 passengers and 61 crewmen), there were 36 passengers.
title: Hindenburg disaster

text: Tami Lynn, an American soul singer born in 1942 in Gert Town, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States, achieved a Top Ten hit on the UK Singles Chart in 1971 with the song "I'm Gonna Run Away From You".
title: Tami Lynn

text: In the film *Black Mass*, actress Dakota Johnson portrays Whitey Bulger's longtime former girlfriend, Lindsey Cyr.
title: Black Mass (film)

text: Popcorn became a popular concession at movie theaters during the Great Depression and gained even more traction during World War II when sugar rationing reduced candy availability. Though theater owners initially objected to the distraction it caused during films, the trend shifted when Glen W. Dickson, a Midwestern theater owner, installed popcorn machines in the lobbies of his theaters in 1938. The venture was a financial success, and the practice quickly spread across the industry. Glen W. Dickson is credited with introducing popcorn machines to movie theaters.
title: Popcorn

text: The rule of the Directory was characterised by suspended elections, debt repudiations, financial instability, persecutions against the Catholic clergy, and significant military conquests abroad. Dogged by charges of corruption, the Directory collapsed in a coup led by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1799. Napoleon, who became the hero of the Revolution through his popular military campaigns, went on to establish the Consulate and later the First Empire, setting the stage for a wider array of global conflicts in the Napoleonic Wars.
title: French Revolution

text: Touching Evil is a British television drama serial that originally aired from 1997 to 1999. The series was produced by United Productions for Anglia Television and broadcast on the ITV network. It began with a first episode on 29 April 1997 and concluded on 6 June 1999, after 16 episodes and three seasons. The first season comprised six 50-minute episodes, and the show's popularity led to two sequel series in 1998 and 1999, though these were not written by the original creators Paul Abbott or Russell T Davies. The total number of episodes in the series is 16.
title: Touching Evil

text:
"A White Sport Coat (and a Pink Carnation)" is a 1957 country and western song with words and music both written by Marty Robbins. The song was recorded on January 25, 1957, and released on March 4 by Columbia Records. Marty Robbins had demanded that Ray Conniff oversee the recording, following the chart success of Guy Mitchell's cover version of his earlier hit "Singing the Blues," which had been scored and conducted by Conniff in October 1956.  
Marty Robbins
title: A White Sport Coat

text: The first high-level language operating system was developed at IBM.
title: History of programming languages

text: Matthew Lyn Lillard, born on January 24, 1970, is an American actor, voice actor, director, and producer best known for his role as Shaggy Rogers in both Scooby-Doo (2002) and Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed (2004). He has been the current voice of Shaggy since veteran actor Casey Kasem retired from the role.
title: Matthew Lillard

text: Real Madrid holds the record for the most victories in the Champions League/European Cup, with 12 titles, including the inaugural competition. They have also won the competition the most times in a row, winning it five times from 1956 to 1960. Five times is the number of consecutive wins Real Madrid achieved during that period.
title: List of European Cup and UEFA Champions League finals

text: A cashier's check is a type of cheque that is guaranteed by a bank, drawn on the bank's own funds and signed by a cashier. This makes it a reliable form of payment, as the bank, not the purchaser, is responsible for fulfilling the payment obligation. These checks are often used in real estate and brokerage transactions. You get a cashier's check from a bank.
title: Cashier's check

text: A cashier's check is issued by a bank, which debits the customer's account immediately and takes responsibility for covering the check. This process distinguishes it from a personal check, where the bank only deducts funds after the check is deposited or cashed. You get a cashier's check from a bank.
title: Cashier's check

text: The FaZe Clan originated on YouTube in 2010 as a group known for trick shots in Call of Duty, later expanding into vlogs and creative content. Members such as FaZe Banks, FaZe Apex, FaZe Blaze, FaZe Rug, FaZe Adapt, FaZe Censor, and FaZe Rain built their individual channels to grow the FaZe brand and engage fans. While these YouTubers are well-known, they do not participate in competitive gaming for the clan. Each major FaZe member currently has over 1 million subscribers on YouTube, with some reaching between three and five million. The official FaZe Clan YouTube channel has 4.8 million subscribers, and FaZe Rug has the most subscribers out of all the FaZe Members with 8 million subscribers.
title: FaZe Clan

text: "Just When I Needed You Most" is a 1979 hit single performed by the American singer-songwriter Randy VanWarmer.
title: Just When I Needed You Most

text: Fluoride ions in saliva and plaque fluid exert a topical effect by forming a fluorapatite-like remineralized veneer over the surface of the enamel. This veneer, which forms when fluoride ions are present in plaque fluid along with dissolved hydroxyapatite and the pH is higher than 4.5, is much more acid-resistant than the original hydroxyapatite and is formed more quickly than ordinary remineralized enamel. The cavity-prevention effect of fluoride is mostly due to these surface effects, which occur during and after tooth eruption. The highest level of fluoride is stored on the surface of the enamel.
title: Water fluoridation

text: In the early 1800s, California society was shaped by Spanish presence, particularly through the expansion of missions, ranches, and military outposts along the southern and central coast. By 1820, Spanish influence was clearly evident in the chain of missions stretching from Loreto to San Diego, and extending inland up to 25 to 50 miles from the coast. Spanish control defined the social and political structure of the region during this period.
title: History of California before 1900

text: Hugh S. Johnson was appointed to manage the National Recovery Administration, serving as its first director. A retired United States Army general and a successful businessman, Johnson was named Time magazine's "Man of the Year" in 1933. He viewed the NRA as a national crusade designed to restore employment and regenerate industry.
title: National Recovery Administration

text: The Paraguay River is a major river in south-central South America, flowing through Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina. It stretches approximately 2,621 kilometres (1,629 mi) from its headwaters in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso to its confluence with the Paraná River north of Corrientes and Resistencia.
title: Paraguay River

text: The Olympic Hymn is traditionally associated with the language of Greece, and in official ceremonies, Greek has been performed despite the host country's official language. For example, during the 2008 Olympic opening and closing ceremonies in Beijing, China, Greek was sung instead of Mandarin, the official language of the host nation. Similarly, in the 2016 Olympic opening ceremonies in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, English was performed instead of Portuguese. Greek remains the language in which the Olympic anthem is officially sung.
title: Olympic Hymn

text: The battle between the USS Bonhomme Richard and the HMS Serapis took place near Flamborough Head on 23 September 1779. The two ships engaged in a fierce fight that lasted four hours, beginning around 6:00 p.m. and ending with the British captain’s surrender at about 10:30 p.m. Despite being heavily damaged, on fire, and leaking, the Bonhomme Richard continued to resist until it sank approximately 36 hours later at 11:00 a.m. on 25 September 1779.
title: USS Bonhomme Richard (1765)

text: Michael Moriarty, best known for his role as Executive Assistant District Attorney Benjamin Stone on the television show Law & Order, portrayed the character during the show's first four seasons from 1990 to 1994. He is also recognized for his earlier work as a Nazi SS officer in the 1978 mini-series Holocaust, for which he earned an Emmy Award and a Golden Globe Award. Moriarty, born on April 5, 1941, is an American-Canadian stage and screen actor and jazz musician, with additional film credits including Bang the Drum Slowly, Who'll Stop the Rain, Q: The Winged Serpent, The Stuff, Pale Rider, Troll, Courage Under Fire, and Shiloh.
title: Michael Moriarty

text: In Return of the Jedi, Leia is revealed to be Vader's daughter and the twin sister of Luke Skywalker.
title: Princess Leia

text: Little Red Riding Hood is a European fairy tale that has its roots in folk traditions dating back to the 10th century, with early versions such as The False Grandmother (Italian: La finta nonna) appearing in Italy. Among the most well-known retellings, the story was written by Charles Perrault. The best known versions were written by Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm.
title: Little Red Riding Hood

text: In the 1697 collection Tales and Stories of the Past with Morals. Tales of Mother Goose (Histoires et contes du temps passé, avec des moralités. Contes de ma mère l'Oye), Charles Perrault included a version of the story known as Le Petit Chaperon Rouge, which became the earliest known printed form of Little Red Riding Hood. This version is both more sinister and more overtly moralized than later adaptations, and it is in this version that the redness of the hood was first introduced as a symbolic detail. The original title and the authorship of this foundational version are directly attributed to Charles Perrault.
title: Little Red Riding Hood

text: The University of Miami, commonly known as UM or The U, is a private, nonsectarian research university located in Coral Gables, Florida. As of 2016, the university enrolls 16,801 students in 12 separate colleges and schools.
title: University of Miami

text: Real images formed by a concave mirror are inverted when the object is located beyond the focal point.
title: Real image

text: In October 2012, Beats unveiled its first two self-developed products, "Beats Executive" headphones and "Beats Pill" wireless speakers—Iovine believed that the company would now have to "control [its] own destiny" in order to continue its growth.
title: Beats Electronics

text: The Crossing, an American science fiction thriller series broadcast on ABC and CTV, was filmed in British Columbia, Canada. The show premiered on April 2, 2018, with the pilot episode made available on ABC's website on March 20, 2018.
title: The Crossing (TV series)

text: The film Cool Hand Luke, released in 1967, follows the story of a prisoner named Luke who resists the oppressive rules of a Florida prison camp. Directed by Stuart Rosenberg and starring Paul Newman in the lead role, it becomes a notable entry in American prison drama cinema. The film was released in 1967.
title: Cool Hand Luke

text: The Hero World Challenge has been held at the Albany development in the Bahamas since 2015, with the event taking place there for at least three years.
title: Hero World Challenge

text: "Put Your Hand in the Hand" is a gospel pop song composed by Gene MacLellan and first recorded by Canadian singer Anne Murray from her third studio album Honey, Wheat and Laughter. Gene MacLellan composed the song.
title: Put Your Hand in the Hand

text: During the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971, President Yahya Khan played a central role in the political leadership of Pakistan. On 25 March 1971, following the "Bihari massacre" in Chittagong and the resignation of Lieutenant-General Yaqub Ali Khan, President Yahya Khan authorized the military to intervene in East Pakistan, deploying forces that were predominantly composed of West Pakistanis to suppress dissent.
title: Indo-Pakistani War of 1971

text: During the escalating tensions leading up to the 1971 war, President Yahya Khan took decisive action by declaring a state of emergency across Pakistan on 23 November 1971, instructing the population to prepare for conflict. This marked a critical moment in the lead-up to the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971, during which Yahya Khan served as the head of state.
title: Indo-Pakistani War of 1971

text: The music video for "Lips of an Angel," which premiered in early 2007, was directed by Shaun Silva and centers on a late-night phone call between the narrator, Austin Winkler, and his former lover, Emmanuelle Chriqui.
title: Lips of an Angel

text: The Romantic period, as commonly defined in many artistic and literary contexts, is generally recognized to have spanned from 1780 to 1830. While there is variation across countries and media, this timeframe is frequently cited as a standard reference point. In English literature, some scholars have placed the beginning around 1789 or 1798 and the end around 1830, though certain interpretations extend slightly beyond that. Nevertheless, the period typically called Romantic is most consistently associated with the timeframe of 1780–1830.
title: Romanticism

text: "A Thousand Years" is a song by American singer-songwriter Christina Perri and David Hodges, featured on the album The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn — Part 1: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack. The track was released as a digital download on October 18, 2011, worldwide and served as the second single from the album. Christina Perri is the artist who sings "I've loved you for a thousand years."
title: A Thousand Years (Christina Perri song)

text: Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian thief born in Dumenza, Varese, on October 8, 1881, is best known for stealing the Mona Lisa from the Louvre on August 21, 1911. He died in Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, France, on October 8, 1925.
title: Vincenzo Peruggia

text: In the village of Anatevka, Hodel expresses her deep devotion to her beloved, declaring that her home is with him, wherever he may be, even as she remains devoted to her family—singing the song "Far From the Home I Love."
title: Fiddler on the Roof

text: The song "Billy Don't Be a Hero" achieved popularity in 1974, first reaching the UK charts with a performance by Paper Lace before gaining a US hit later that same year with Bo Donaldson and The Heywoods. This track was originally created by British songwriters Mitch Murray and Peter Callander.
title: Billy Don't Be a Hero

text: In the File Transfer Protocol, all transmissions are in clear text, meaning usernames, passwords, commands, and data can be read by anyone who performs packet capture on the network.
title: File Transfer Protocol

text: Pradyumna (Sanskrit: प्रद्युम्न) is a significant figure in Hindu mythology, known as the son of Lord Krishna and Rukmini. He is recognized as one of the four vyuha avatars of Vishnu and is also referred to as Vishnu Ankar Gupta. According to certain traditions, Pradyumna was an incarnation of Kamadeva, the god of love. The name Pradyumna holds a unique place in Sanskrit, being the only name with all three letters joined (referred as जोडाक्षर), and is one of the 24 Keshava Namas, celebrated in all pujas.
title: Pradyumna

text: "I Wanna Be the Only One" is a hit song by the British R&B group Eternal, featured as the third single from their album Before the Rain. The track reached the top of the UK Singles Chart and marked the group's third collaboration with BeBe Winans, who produced their earlier hits "Crazy" in 1994 and "It Will Never End" in 1995. BeBe Winans sang with Eternal on "I Wanna Be the Only One."
title: I Wanna Be the Only One

text: A diastema (plural diastemata) is a space or gap between two teeth, and this gap is particularly noticeable between the center of the two front teeth. In many mammals, diastemata are a normal anatomical feature, often found between the incisors and molars. These gaps are common in children and can persist into adulthood. The presence of a diastema is usually due to an imbalance between the jaw size and the size of the teeth, and in some cases, the labial frenulum (lip tissue) can pull and push the teeth apart, leading to a diastema between the front teeth.
title: Diastema

text: The CN Tower features a metal staircase that reaches the SkyPod, located 100 meters (328 feet) above the main deck, after 2,579 steps. This staircase is the tallest metal staircase on Earth and is intended for emergency use only, though it is occasionally open to the public during charity stair-climb events twice a year. The stairs were originally on the northern side of the tower with a glass view but were later moved to the inside of the core and replaced with a windowless stairwell, which has been in use since around 2003.
title: CN Tower

text: In April 2016, South Sudan signed a treaty of accession to the East African Community, marking a key step in its formal integration process.
title: East African Community

text: In Test cricket, the format changed to six balls per over starting from the 1979/80 season. Since 1979/80, all Test cricket has been played with six balls per over. Prior to this, overs originally had four balls, and the number of balls per over varied globally up to that point, typically matching the standard in other first-class cricket in the respective country.
title: Over (cricket)

text: On the first day of each new Congress and whenever a Speaker dies, resigns, or is removed, the House of Representatives selects a new Speaker. Members of the House submit their votes by naming the candidate they support during a roll call, with the Clerk of the House initiating the process by gathering nominations—typically one from each major party. While representatives are generally expected to vote for a nominated candidate, they are not limited to doing so and may choose any individual, even someone not currently serving in the House. A representative may also choose to vote "present" instead of supporting a candidate.
title: Speaker of the United States House of Representatives

text: In the tenth season of *My Three Sons*, which aired from 1969 to 1970, Steve remarries and takes widowed teacher Barbara Harper as his wife; Beverly Garland plays Barbara Harper. She brings with her a 5-year-old daughter, Dorothy "Dodie," and Steve subsequently adopts her as his stepdaughter.
title: My Three Sons

text: In Chinese mythology, the dragon kings guard the Four Seas, each overseeing a major sea region: the East Sea, the South Sea, the West Sea, and the North Sea.
title: Chinese dragon

text: Naz Khialvi, a renowned Pakistani lyricist and radio broadcaster, is best known for his Sufi verse "Tum Ek Gorakh Dhanda Ho," which translates to "You are a Puzzle" in Urdu. This poetic line, later popularized by the legendary Qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, became a defining piece of his legacy.
title: Naz Khialvi

text: John Hancock, a prominent Patriot during the American Revolution, is best known for his large and stylish signature on the United States Declaration of Independence. His signature on the document is so distinctive that the term "John Hancock" has become a common synonym in the United States for a signature.
title: John Hancock

text: The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, commonly referred to as Rio+20, took place in Rio de Janeiro from 13 to 22 June 2012. This event served as a 20-year follow-up to the 1992 Earth Summit and marked the 10th anniversary of the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development. The summit was hosted by Brazil and brought together global leaders to address sustainable development goals, balancing economic growth with environmental protection. The official dates of the conference are 13 to 22 June 2012.
title: United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development

text: The story of Small Steps is set in Austin, Texas, where Theodore "Armpit" Johnson lives two years after his release from Camp Green Lake, working at the mayor's home and caring for his neighbor Ginny McDonald, a ten-year-old girl with cerebral palsy. Austin, Texas serves as the backdrop for Armpit's efforts to establish a stable life, including his involvement in a money-lending scheme with Rex "X-Ray" Washburn, one of his former camp friends.
title: Small Steps (novel)

text: Pretty Little Liars season 7 consisted of 20 episodes, ten of which aired in the summer of 2016, with the remaining ten airing from April 2017. The season's premiere took place on June 21, 2016, on Freeform. Production began in March 2016, and the season finale was confirmed on August 29, 2016, marking the end of the series.
title: Pretty Little Liars (season 7)

text: The South Pole is located on the continent of Antarctica.
title: South Pole

text: Before 1948, north and south Vietnam were a part of France. In 1947 full-scale war broke out between the Viet Minh and France. Realizing that colonialism was coming to an end worldwide, France fashioned a semi-independent State of Vietnam, within the French Union, with Bảo Đại as Head of State.
title: History of Vietnam since 1945

text: Walmart is a prime example of a multinational retail corporation, operating a global network of hypermarkets, discount department stores, and grocery stores across 28 countries under various regional names. Headquartered in Bentonville, Arkansas, the company was founded by Sam Walton in 1962 and incorporated on October 31, 1969. As of October 31, 2017, Walmart has 11,703 stores and clubs in 28 countries, operating under 59 different names. The company operates under the name Walmart in the United States and Canada, as Walmart de México y Centroamérica in Mexico and Central America, as Asda in the United Kingdom, as the Seiyu Group in Japan, and as Best Price in India. It has wholly owned operations in Argentina, Chile, Brazil, and Canada.
title: Walmart

text: Roger Dean Stadium is the spring training home of the Miami Marlins, and it is one of only two stadiums in Florida to host two Major League Baseball teams annually for spring training, including the St. Louis Cardinals. The stadium is shared by both teams, with each having its own practice fields, outdoor batting cages, several pitching mounds, and state-of-the-art conditioning rooms. Roger Dean Stadium is the location where the Florida Marlins conduct their spring training.
title: Roger Dean Stadium

text: The term "social justice" became used explicitly from the 1840s.
title: Social justice

text: The term "social justice" first appeared in the 1840s, notably in the writings of Catholic thinkers such as the Jesuit Luigi Taparelli in Civiltà Cattolica, who drew upon the philosophical foundations of St. Thomas Aquinas to argue against the societal fragmentation caused by capitalist and socialist theories rooted in Cartesian thought.
title: Social justice

text: The law specifying how people should behave during the playing of the National Anthem was revised on June 22, 1942, when it was established that those in uniform should salute, while others should stand at attention and remove their hats.
title: The Star-Spangled Banner

text: Dolley Madison risked her life to save iconic treasures during the War of 1812 and set the standard for the role. She popularized the First Ladyship through her efforts to assist orphans and women, her elegant fashion choices, and her active engagement with public life, becoming the model for nearly every First Lady until Eleanor Roosevelt in the 1930s.
title: First Lady of the United States

text: In Middle-Eastern cuisine, clarified butter is traditionally known as smen and is widely used as a preferred cooking medium.
title: Middle-Eastern cuisine

text: Phosphorus pentoxide is a chemical compound with molecular formula P4O10 (with its common name derived from its empirical formula, P2O5). This white crystalline solid is the anhydride of phosphoric acid and functions as a powerful desiccant and dehydrating agent.
title: Phosphorus pentoxide

text: Spirit of the Suwannee Music Park is owned by The Cornett family, who have been actively making improvements to the park to enhance and improve its entertainment, hiking, canoeing, camping, and other activities. The park provides a range of camping options, including primitive camping, RV camping, and furnished park models, and also features a tree house available for various occasions and events.
title: Spirit of the Suwannee Music Park

text: In the original version of Return of the Jedi, Sebastian Shaw portrayed an unmasked and redeemed Anakin Skywalker (formerly Darth Vader), and his ghost appears in the film.
title: Sebastian Shaw (actor)

text: In the pivotal scene aboard Death Star II, the actor Sebastian Shaw portrays the unmasked and dying Anakin Skywalker, revealing the identity behind the mask of Darth Vader.
title: Sebastian Shaw (actor)

text: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, the first book in the Harry Potter series, was first published in 1997 by Bloomsbury.
title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

text: James P. Flynn played the judge in the Boston-based film Good Will Hunting in 1997. Known in show business as James P. Flynn, he appeared in several films shot in the New England area, including The Cider House Rules in 1999 and What's the Worst That Could Happen? in 2001. He also served as a truck driver for movie production equipment during the filming of My Best Friend's Girl in 2008, and Boston actor Tom Kemp noted that [The film The Departed] wouldn't be a Boston movie without me, a Wahlberg, and Jimmy Flynn from the teamsters.
title: Jimmy Flynn

text: The first session of the Assam Association was held in Guwahati in 1905. This marked a significant milestone in the region's political awakening, setting the stage for future organizational activities in the area. Guwahati remained a central hub for political gatherings and discussions during that period.
title: Tarun Ram Phukan

text: "Does He Love You" is a country music song written by Sandy Knox and Billy Stritch, performed as a duet by Reba McEntire and Linda Davis. The track was released in August 1993 as the lead single from Reba's album Greatest Hits Volume Two and is part of a collection of country songs exploring themes of love triangles. Linda Davis is one of the artists who sang the song with Reba McEntire.
title: Does He Love You

text: Accounts receivable arises from invoices issued by a business to customers for goods supplied or services rendered, which are delivered for payment within an agreed time frame. These invoices serve as the primary source of information for accounts receivable.
title: Accounts receivable

text: In the film *The Lost City of Z*, Manley dies in the trenches at the Battle of the Somme.
title: The Lost City of Z (film)

text: Hydrogen peroxide is produced as a temporary byproduct in biochemical reactions within nearly all living cells, where it can be harmful due to its ability to oxidize proteins, membrane lipids, and DNA. To counteract this, cells produce the enzyme superoxide dismutase, which is present in nearly all living cells, to convert superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which is then quickly broken down by catalase into oxygen and water.
title: Hydrogen peroxide

text: The UK legislation that safeguards personal data whether it is stored electronically or in a structured paper archive is the Data Protection Act 1998. This law was developed to align with the EU Data Protection Directive 1995, establishing clear rules for how personal information is handled, processed, and transferred. It grants individuals specific rights over their personal details, ensuring they can control how their data is used. While the Act does not extend to private, household-level uses—like maintaining a personal address book—it applies to anyone managing personal data for business or organizational purposes, with certain exceptions. The framework is built upon eight core principles that govern lawful data processing.
title: Data Protection Act 1998

text: Eurostar trains arrive in London at St Pancras International, which serves as the primary terminus for services into the UK. Other British stations include Ebbsfleet International and Ashford International in Kent.
title: Eurostar

text: Krypton-85 undergoes decay primarily through the emission of a beta particle, resulting in the formation of rubidium-85. This decay process is the dominant pathway, occurring in 99.57% of cases, and produces rubidium-85 as the product. The decay is accompanied by a maximum energy of 687 keV and an average energy of 251 keV for the beta particles. A minor fraction, 0.43%, decays via beta emission followed by gamma emission, but the primary product remains rubidium-85.
title: Krypton-85

text: "Every Light in the House" is a song written by Kent Robbins and recorded by American country music artist Trace Adkins. It was released in August 1996 as the second single from his debut album Dreamin' Out Loud. Trace Adkins achieved his first Top 5 hit on the Hot Country Singles & Tracks (now Hot Country Songs) chart with this song, where it reached #3.
title: Every Light in the House

text: Lowe's, based in Toronto, Ontario, began its Canadian operations with three stores opening on December 10, 2007, in Hamilton, Brampton, and Brantford. Additional stores followed, including three openings on February 1, 2008, in Toronto, East Gwillimbury, a second Brampton location, and Maple (Vaughan). As of 2018, Lowe's has 62 locations in Canada. The company has expanded into Western Canada with three new stores in Calgary, Alberta, with one opening in late September 2010 and the other two in early 2011, bringing stores to British Columbia, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan.
title: Lowe's

text: The central processing unit (CPU) concept was foundational to the development of stored-program computers, and this idea was formally articulated by mathematician John von Neumann in his 1945 report titled "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC." Von Neumann proposed that programs should be stored in high-speed memory rather than being hardwired into the computer, a design principle that became central to the architecture of modern CPUs. This approach allowed for flexible and efficient computation, enabling the program to be changed simply by altering the memory contents. John von Neumann is credited with developing the central processing unit (CPU).
title: Central processing unit

text: In the book of Acts, the twelve disciples are mentioned in Acts 1:13, where it states that they were gathered together in Jerusalem after Jesus’ resurrection. This passage confirms the presence of the twelve apostles in that location, providing a clear reference to their group at that time.

text: Anna Muttathupadathu, later known as Saint Alphonsa, became the first Indian woman to be canonized as a saint by the Catholic Church. Her sainthood was formally recognized on 28 July 1946, the date of her passing, and her feast day is celebrated annually on that day. text: The harp is recognized as the arms of Ireland, a designation first recorded in the Wijnbergen Roll from around 1280, which attributed "D'azure a la harpe d'or" to the King of Ireland. This symbol, traditionally linked to King David, appears rarely in medieval arms and is found in only two of 19 early rolls. While its origins remain debated—possibly stemming from a fictional character in the Tristan legend or a 13th-century bardic poem dedicated to a Gaelic king—the harp has remained a central emblem in Ireland's heraldic identity.
title: Coat of arms of Ireland

text: The song "How Do You Do It?" was written by Mitch Murray, who offered it to Adam Faith and Brian Poole but was turned down. George Martin of EMI decided to pick it up for the new group he was producing, the Beatles, as the A-side of their first record. The Beatles recorded the song but opposed releasing it, feeling that it did not fit their sound, but worked out changes from Murray's demo-disc version. These included a new introduction, vocal harmony, an instrumental interlude, small lyric changes and removal of the half-step modulation for the last verse. They recorded the song in September, 1962; although Murray disliked their changes, the decision not to release the Beatles' version was primarily a business one. "Love Me Do" was their first single instead. The recording was officially released in November 1995 on the Beatles retrospective Anthology 1 album. Mitch Murray

text: During the shift from command to market economies in Central and Eastern Europe, inequality of opportunity emerged as a significant outcome, particularly in regions like the Balkans and Central Asia. This measure of inequality was higher in these transition economies compared to several Western European developed nations, except France, where it remained relatively high. While access to education and health services showed relatively low gender-based disparities, labor practices, employment opportunities, entrepreneurship, and access to finance exhibited medium to high levels of inequality. In Central Asia, women faced notable barriers in accessing health services, similar to patterns observed in Arab countries. Despite strong performance in primary and secondary education, the transition economies lagged in training and tertiary education, further contributing to persistent inequality of opportunity.
title: Transition economy

text:
Gibraltar, a British Overseas Territory situated at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, is the subject of an irredentist territorial claim by Spain. The territory was captured in 1704 during the War of the Spanish Succession and formally ceded to the British Crown in 1713 under Article X of the Treaty of Utrecht. Spain has on multiple occasions attempted to recapture Gibraltar, including during the thirteenth siege in 1727 and the Great siege from 1779 to 1783. British sovereignty over Gibraltar was reaffirmed in later treaties signed in Seville (1729) and the Treaty of Paris (1783).  
Gibraltar
title: Disputed status of Gibraltar

text: The territory in dispute between Spain and the United Kingdom is Gibraltar. The Gibraltarians themselves reject any claim of union with Spain, and no political party or pressure group in Gibraltar supports such a union. In a referendum in 2002, the people of Gibraltar rejected a joint sovereignty proposal on which Spain and the United Kingdom were said to have reached "broad agreement". The British Government has stated that it would "never ... enter into an agreement on sovereignty without the agreement of the Government of Gibraltar and their people". The British Government now refuses to discuss sovereignty without the consent of the Gibraltarians.
title: Disputed status of Gibraltar

text: Gibraltar is a territory where Spain and the United Kingdom are in dispute, with Spain challenging the legality of the Gibraltar Constitution Order 2006 and asserting that Gibraltar remains a British colony with only the UK having the authority to address international matters concerning the territory.

text: The dermis, also known as the corium, lies between the epidermis and the subcutaneous tissues, forming the cutis with the epidermis. It is divided into two layers: the superficial area adjacent to the epidermis, called the papillary region, and a deeper, thicker layer known as the reticular dermis. This layer is tightly connected to the epidermis through a basement membrane. Structural components include collagen, elastic fibers, and extrafibrillar matrix, and it houses mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors that contribute to sensory perception. Additionally, the dermis contains hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands, apocrine glands, lymphatic vessels, and blood vessels that support both dermal and epidermal cells. The papillary region is specifically described as being adjacent to the epidermis.
title: Dermis

text: Gestalt psychology, rooted in the philosophy of mind of the Berlin School of experimental psychology, emerged as a framework to explore how humans form meaningful perceptions in a chaotic environment. Central to this approach is the idea that the mind naturally organizes experiences into a coherent whole through self-organizing tendencies. Despite its influence, the physiological foundations of Gestalt theory remain poorly defined, and critics argue that the theory describes the outcomes of perception without clearly explaining the underlying processes. As noted in a 2016 special issue of Vision Research, even though modern studies examine similar phenomena, there is little theoretical coherence, raising questions about the continuity of the Gestalt school’s original vision. The Berlin School of experimental psychology remains a key reference point for understanding the origins and development of gestalt psychology.
title: Gestalt psychology

The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire, known as "Tahuantinsuyu" or "Tawantinsuyu" in Quechua, meaning "Realm of the Four Parts," was a pivotal event in the Spanish colonization of the Americas. Following years of exploration and skirmishes, 180 Spanish soldiers led by conquistador Francisco Pizarro, along with his brothers and native allies, captured the Sapa Inca Atahualpa in the 1532 Battle of Cajamarca. This marked the beginning of a prolonged campaign that ultimately concluded with Spanish victory in 1572 and the establishment of the Viceroyalty of Peru. The conquest led to further military expansions into modern-day Chile and Colombia, as well as expeditions into the Amazon Basin.  
**conquistador Francisco Pizarro** was the leader of the conquest of the Inca Empire.

text:
Sockeye salmon, known also as red salmon, kokanee salmon, or blueback salmon, are an anadromous species native to the Northern Pacific Ocean and the rivers that flow into it. This fish is primarily red in color during spawning and can grow up to 84 cm (2 ft 9 in) in length, weighing between 2.3 and 7 kg (5.1–15.4 lb). Juveniles stay in freshwater until they are ready to migrate to the ocean, traveling distances of up to 1,600 km (990 mi). Their diet mainly consists of zooplankton, and they are semelparous, meaning they die after spawning. Some populations, called kokanee, remain in freshwater their entire lives and do not migrate to the ocean.  
the Northern Pacific Ocean
title: Sockeye salmon

text: In the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, proinsulin undergoes post translational modification to become mature insulin. During this process, as proinsulin is transported through the Golgi apparatus, the C-peptide is cleaved with the help of two endoproteases: Type I endoproteases PC1 and PC3, which disrupt the C peptide-B chain connection, and PC2, a type II endoprotease, which cleaves the C peptide-A chain bond. The resulting molecule, now mature insulin, is stored as a hexamer in secretory vesicles and is stabilized with Zn²⁺ molecules until it is secreted.
title: Proinsulin

text: Fructose, or fruit sugar, is a simple ketonic monosaccharide commonly found in plants, where it often combines with glucose to form sucrose. This sugar is naturally present in honey, tree and vine fruits, flowers, berries, and most root vegetables. Pure, dry fructose appears as a sweet, white, odorless, crystalline solid and is the most water-soluble of all sugars. Fructose is one of the three dietary monosaccharides—along with glucose and galactose—that are absorbed directly into the bloodstream during digestion.
title: Fructose

text: In statistical hypothesis testing, the type I error rate, also known as the significance level, represents the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. This rate is denoted by α (alpha) and is commonly set at 0.05 (5%), meaning there is a 5% chance of making a type I error when the null hypothesis is retained at the 0.05 level of significance.
title: Type I and type II errors

text: Lōʻihi Seamount, also known as Lōʻihi, is an active submarine volcano located about 35 km (22 mi) off the southeast coast of the island of Hawaii. The top of the seamount lies approximately 975 m (3,000 ft) below sea level and sits on the flank of Mauna Loa, the largest shield volcano on Earth. Lōʻihi is the newest volcano in the Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain, a long chain of volcanoes that extends over 5,800 km (3,600 mi) northwest of Lōʻihi. Unlike most active volcanoes in the Pacific Ocean found along plate boundaries in the Pacific Ring of Fire, Lōʻihi and the other volcanoes in this chain are hotspot volcanoes and formed well away from the nearest plate boundary. Volcanoes in the Hawaiian Islands arise from the Hawaii hotspot, and as the youngest volcano in the chain, Lōʻihi is the only Hawaiian volcano in the deep submarine preshield stage of development. from the Hawaii hotspot
title: Lōʻihi Seamount

text: The song "The Windmills of Your Mind" originally appears in the 1968 film *The Thomas Crown Affair*, where it is sung by Noel Harrison during the opening credits and in a scene featuring the character Thomas Crown flying a glider at a glider airport in Salem, New Hampshire. The track was commissioned by director Norman Jewison after he used the Beatles' "Strawberry Fields Forever" as a reference for the glider scene, seeking an original composition that captured the character’s conflicted emotions. Composer Michel Legrand presented several melodies, and the team of Alan Bergman and Marilyn Bergman selected one—a long baroque melody—whose lyrics were developed in a stream-of-consciousness manner to evoke a mental journey. The title was initially a line at the end of a section, and after the song was completed, the team realized its significance, restructured it so the line returned at the end, and ultimately named it "The Windmills of Your Mind," inspired by the feeling of thoughts and memories tumbling when trying to fall asleep. text: Appropriation bills, which authorize the spending of public funds, fall under Congress's power to raise revenue. The process involves both chambers drafting their own versions, with the Senate then "cutting-and-pasting" its version into the House bill before final agreement. The power to raise revenue encompasses not only taxation but also the authority to allocate funds through appropriation bills.
title: Appropriation bill

text: Apoptosis is a tightly controlled process that begins only when specific signals are received. It can be triggered through two main pathways: the intrinsic pathway, where the cell detects internal stress and initiates self-destruction, and the extrinsic pathway, where the cell receives signals from other cells. These signals from other cells are a key factor in initiating apoptosis. Both pathways ultimately lead to cell death by activating caspases, enzymes that break down proteins. The extrinsic pathway specifically relies on external cues, confirming that the signals for apoptosis come from other cells.
title: Apoptosis

text: The objective correlative, a concept central to literary theory, was significantly developed by the poet and literary critic T.S. Eliot. In his essay "Hamlet and His Problems," republished in *The Sacred Wood: Essays on Poetry and Criticism*, Eliot outlines his view of Shakespeare's incomplete emotional development in *Hamlet*, using Lady Macbeth's state of mind as an example of the successful objective correlative: "The artistic 'inevitability' lies in this complete adequacy of the external to the emotion…." This approach contrasts with Hamlet’s emotional portrayal, which Eliot argues lacks sufficient external support. Eliot's theory emphasizes expressing character emotions through external elements rather than direct description, aligning with the ancient distinction between mimesis and diegesis first proposed by Plato. The objective correlative, as defined by Eliot, enables the author to remain detached from the character while still conveying the emotion effectively.
title: Objective correlative

text: Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from Mainz, Germany, is credited with inventing the first metal movable-type printing system in Europe. This innovation made it possible to cast large quantities of movable type, allowing for the practical printing of complete books. Johannes Gutenberg is thus recognized as the pioneer who established movable-type printing in Europe.

text: Trigger points form only in muscles. They develop as a local contraction in a small number of muscle fibers within a larger muscle or muscle bundle. These contractions can pull on tendons and ligaments associated with the muscle and may lead to pain deep within a joint where no muscles are present. The integrated hypothesis theory suggests that trigger points arise from excessive release of acetylcholine, resulting in sustained depolarization of muscle fibers. Indeed, the trigger point has an abnormal biochemical composition with elevated concentrations of acetylcholine, noradrenaline and serotonin and a lower pH. These sustained contractions compress the local blood supply, restricting energy availability in the region, which leads to the production of sensitizing substances that interact with nociceptive nerves in the area, ultimately causing localized pain within the muscle at the neuromuscular junction. When trigger points are present in muscles, pain and weakness in associated structures are often observed. The pain patterns in muscles follow specific nerve pathways and have been mapped to identify the causative pain factor. Many trigger points exhibit overlapping pain patterns, and some create reciprocal cyclic relationships that require extensive treatment to resolve.
title: Myofascial trigger point

text: David Ben-Gurion, as leader of the Yishuv, was the first person to sign the Israeli Declaration of Independence. The declaration was intended to be signed by all 37 members of Moetzet HaAm, though twelve could not attend—eleven were trapped in besieged Jerusalem and one was abroad. The remaining 25 signatories present were called up in alphabetical order to sign, with spaces left for those absent. Although a space was left for him between the signatures of Eliyahu Dobkin and Meir Vilner, Zerach Warhaftig signed at the top of the next column, leading to speculation that Vilner's name had been left alone to isolate him, or to stress that even a communist agreed with the declaration. However, Warhaftig later denied this, stating that a space had been left for him (as he was one of the signatories trapped in Jerusalem) where a Hebraicised form of his name would have fitted alphabetically, but he insisted on signing under his actual name so as to honour his father's memory and so moved down two spaces. He and Vilner would be the last surviving signatories, and remained close for the rest of their lives. Of the signatories, two were women (Golda Meir (Meyerson/Myerson) and Rachel Cohen-Kagan). David Ben-Gurion was the first signatory of the Israeli Declaration of Independence.
title: Israeli Declaration of Independence

text: The most common form of megalithic architecture in Europe is the portal tomb – a chamber consisting of upright stones (orthostats) with one or more large flat capstones forming a roof. While many of these structures contain human remains, it remains uncertain whether their primary function was as burial sites. Though often referred to as dolmens, the term accepted by archaeologists is portal tomb. Various regional names exist for this type of structure, including anta in Galicia and Portugal, stazzone in Sardinia, hunebed in the Netherlands, Hünengrab in Germany, dysse in Denmark, and cromlech in Wales. It is generally believed that most portal tombs were originally covered by earthen mounds.
title: Megalith

After a confrontation involving a cudgel, Robin finally learns that Major Molineux will soon pass by. He waits at the church steps, where he meets his first friendly person all night, only to later witness a mob charging toward them, led by the same strange man and including Major Molineux, who is tarred and feathered. The crowd erupts in laughter, and Robin, too, begins to smile when he sees the major, who instantly recognizes him. Disillusioned, he asks the gentleman for directions back to the ferry, but is stopped, told that life might still flourish without the protection of his kinsman. text: In 1989, university education in Australia began to introduce fees through the implementation of the Higher Education Contributions Scheme (HECS). The HECS system was first proposed by Professor Murray Wells and later developed by Bruce Chapman, with support from Education Minister John Dawkins. Under the original scheme, a $1,800 fee was charged to all university students, with the Commonwealth covering the remainder. Students could defer payment, creating a HECS debt, which would be repaid later through the tax system when their income exceeded a certain threshold. This reform initiated a shift from free university education to a system with tuition contributions, and the HECS system has remained in place since, though with modifications.

text: The Prince-Electors were the German princes who held the authority to choose the Holy Roman Emperor. From the 13th century onward, they played a central role in electing the King of the Romans, who would later be crowned as Holy Roman Emperor by the Pope. This electoral process continued until Charles V, who was elected in 1519 and crowned in 1530, marking the last time an Emperor was formally crowned. After that, each subsequent Emperor was elected directly by the electoral college and referred to as "Elected Emperor of the Romans" (German: erwählter Römischer Kaiser; Latin: electus Romanorum imperator). While the Electors formally participated in the selection, from 1440 onward, all but one Emperor—Charles VII of the House of Wittelsbach—came from the Austrian House of Habsburg, with the Electors essentially ratifying the Habsburg succession.
title: Prince-elector

text: Among the various accounts of the final moments aboard the RMS Titanic, one of the most cited tunes is "Autumn," according to wireless operator Harold Bride, who was close enough to the ship’s band to hear them before it sank. While some passengers, like Mrs. Vera Dick, claimed the final song was the hymn "Nearer, My God, to Thee," Bride’s testimony—recorded in the aftermath of the disaster—specifically mentions hearing "Autumn" as the last piece played. Though the exact nature of the song remains debated, with some suggesting it might refer to the hymn tune known as "Autumn" or the waltz "Songe d'Automne," neither appears in the White Star Line’s official songbook. Given that Bride was one of the few witnesses physically near the band during the final moments, his account is regarded by some as credible. The idea that the band performed "Nearer, My God, to Thee" as a farewell may stem from a different maritime incident, the wreck of the SS Valencia in 1906, which may have influenced passenger memories. Nonetheless, the only verifiable reference to a final song from a direct observer is the mention of "Autumn."
title: Legends and myths regarding RMS Titanic

text: Iron ore in Australia is primarily sourced from Western Australia, which accounts for the vast majority of the country's production. In 2011, Western Australia produced 474 million tonnes of iron ore, representing 97% of Australia's total output. The state holds the world's largest Economic Demonstrated Resources of iron ore, making up 22% of global reserves. Much of this ore is exported to China, which imported 70 percent of Western Australia's 2010 production, followed by Japan at 19% and South Korea at 10%. Western Australia is thus the main origin of iron ore in Australia.
title: Iron ore mining in Western Australia

text: Iron ore mining in Western Australia began in earnest in 1960 after the Australian Government lifted its export embargo on iron ore. Although iron ore deposits were known earlier, such as the Mount Whaleback deposit discovered in 1957, production remained negligible until the mid-1960s, with output below 10 million tonnes annually. By the mid-1970s, production had surged to 100 million tonnes, with the majority coming from Western Australia. While output dipped in the 1980s, it recovered in the 1990s, reaching 150 million tonnes nationally by 1997 and 200 million tonnes by 2003. Western Australia remains a primary source of iron ore in Australia.
title: Iron ore mining in Western Australia

text: Enacted in 1953 as the Bantu Education Act—later known as the Black Education Act—the law formalized the apartheid regime’s policy of racial segregation in education. A central component of this legislation was enforcing racially separated educational facilities. This meant that schools and universities were structured along racial lines, with African students receiving inferior curricula and limited access to higher education. The government systematically dismantled independent institutions, closing most missionary schools and shifting educational funding away from native communities. Even prestigious institutions like Fort Hare were absorbed into the system and downgraded to serve the Bantu education framework. While some argued the policy was designed to funnel black youth into unskilled labor, the official rationale, as stated by Minister Hendrik Verwoerd, focused on resolving South Africa’s ethnic tensions through the creation of distinct economic and political units.
title: Bantu Education Act, 1953

text: The Indian National Congress, established in 1885, emerged as the first modern nationalist movement in the British Empire across Asia and Africa. From the late 19th century, and especially after 1920, under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, Congress became the principal leader of the Indian independence movement, with over 15 million members and over 70 million participants. Mahatma Gandhi played a central role in shaping the movement, guiding Congress to lead India to independence from Great Britain and significantly influencing other anti-colonial nationalist movements within the British Empire.
title: Indian National Congress

text: Alan Turing was a central figure in breaking the Enigma code during World War II. While working at Bletchley Park for the Government Code and Cypher School, he led Hut 8, the section responsible for German naval cryptanalysis, and devised several techniques to speed up the decryption of German ciphers, including improvements to the pre-war Polish bombe method. Turing played a pivotal role in cracking intercepted coded messages, which enabled the Allies to defeat the Nazis in key battles such as the Battle of the Atlantic. His contributions were instrumental in helping win the war. Turing.
title: Alan Turing

text: Blond hair is a rare trait in adult populations, with natural light blond hair occurring in only about 2% of the global population. This figure is supported by historical estimates that place the proportion of naturally blond individuals at 2%, though regional variations exist. While blond hair is most prevalent among Northern and Western European populations, it can be found across much of Europe and beyond. In certain regions like the Solomon Islands, a recessive genetic mutation in the tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TYRP1) gene leads to naturally blond hair, with 26% of the local population carrying the gene—though this mutation is limited to Oceania. Despite these regional differences, the global baseline for naturally blond hair remains consistently cited at 2%.
title: Human hair color

text: In cars and various vehicles, a mirror is commonly installed to help the driver view the area behind the vehicle. The rear-view mirror is a standard feature in most vehicles, ensuring safe and effective navigation.
title: Rear-view mirror

text: The rear-view mirror is a standard feature in vehicles, typically mounted on the top of the windshield using a double-swivel mount. title: Rear-view mirror

text: When considering a nomination to the Supreme Court, the Senate must vote on the nominee, and a simple majority vote is required to confirm or to reject the nominee. This means that just over half of the Senate's members must vote in favor for confirmation. While prior to 2017, a filibuster could have required a supermajority of 60 to end debate and proceed to a final vote, the current standard for confirmation remains a simple majority vote.
title: Appointment and confirmation to the Supreme Court of the United States

text: When Einstein received his Nobel Prize in 1921, it was not for his more difficult and mathematically laborious special and general relativity, but for the simple, yet totally revolutionary, suggestion of quantized light. Einstein's "light quanta" would not be called photons until 1925, but even in 1905 they represented the quintessential example of wave-particle duality. Electromagnetic radiation propagates following linear wave equations, but can only be emitted or absorbed as discrete elements, thus acting as a wave and a particle simultaneously.
title: Wave–particle duality

text: A direct transition from a gaseous state to a solid state, bypassing the liquid phase, is known as deposition. This process is also referred to as desublimation in some contexts.
title: Deposition (phase transition)

text: pH, or potential of hydrogen, is a numeric scale used to specify the acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution. It is approximately the negative of the base 10 logarithm of the molar concentration, measured in units of moles per liter, of hydrogen ions. More precisely it is the negative of the base 10 logarithm of the activity of the hydrogen ion. Solutions with a pH less than 7 are acidic and solutions with a pH greater than 7 are basic. Pure water is neutral, at pH 7 (25 °C), being neither an acid nor a base. Contrary to popular belief, the pH value can be less than 0 or greater than 14 for very strong acids and bases respectively.
title: pH

text: Fold mountains develop at a convergent plate boundary where two tectonic plates move toward each other. This process involves sedimentary rocks that build up along continental margins, which then crumple and fold under the pressure of the colliding plates, much like a tablecloth being pushed across a table—especially when a mechanically weak layer, such as salt, is present. A convergent plate boundary is responsible for the folded mountains of Pennsylvania and the high Himalayas.
title: Fold mountains

title: Chicago Tylenol murders

text: Vincent van Gogh created two series of still life paintings known as Sunflowers. The first was painted in Paris in 1887, featuring sunflowers laid on the ground, while the second, completed the following year in Arles, portrayed a bouquet of sunflowers arranged in a vase. These two series were deeply connected in van Gogh’s mind, partly due to his friend Paul Gauguin, who had acquired two of the Paris versions. The artist later envisioned the two major versions as wings of a triptych called the Berceuse, and eventually displayed them in the Les XX exhibition in Bruxelles. The name Sunflowers, originally in French as Tournesols, refers to these two distinct series.
title: Sunflowers (Van Gogh series)

text: In the summer of 1914, a pivotal event unfolded in Sarajevo when Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was fatally wounded during a public visit. Alongside his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, he was killed by Gavrilo Princip, one of several conspirators linked to a nationalist movement seeking to unify South Slavic territories. The group, organized by Danilo Ilić of the Black Hand, included five Serbs and one Bosniak, all acting under the political goal of severing Austria-Hungary’s control over its Slavic provinces. This act directly precipitated the outbreak of the First World War after Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia, which was only partially accepted. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria remains a defining moment in 20th-century European history.
title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria

text: In many kinds of organs, surface area is important because the amount of surface determines effective gas exchange. This is especially true in larger organisms, which have a small surface-area to volume ratio, and rely on specialised structures with convoluted surfaces—such as gills, pulmonary alveoli, and spongy mesophyll—to provide the large area needed for effective gas exchange. These structures often form internal surfaces within the body, like the alveoli in mammalian lungs or the spongy mesophyll in plant leaves, to maximise the efficiency of gas exchange.
title: Gas exchange

text: Sedimentary rock dominates the Earth's surface, covering 73% of the current land surface of the continents. Although sedimentary rocks make up only 8% of the total volume of the Earth's crust, they form a widespread and extensive layer across the planet's land areas. These rocks are deposited in layers known as strata, creating a structure called bedding. The presence and study of sedimentary rocks provide valuable insights into the subsurface, supporting applications in civil engineering such as road and tunnel construction. Sedimentary rocks also serve as key sources of natural resources including coal, fossil fuels, drinking water, and ores.
title: Sedimentary rock

text: In the early 16th century, German cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann, aided by René II, Duke of Lorraine, compiled extensive geographic data from recent explorations to create a new comprehensive map of the world. For the first time in history, they applied the name America to a map, based on the belief that the landmass discovered by Amerigo Vespucci was a new continent—not just a collection of islands as Christopher Columbus had found. This naming decision reflected the growing recognition of Vespucci’s voyages as pivotal in identifying a vast, continuous landmass in the Western Hemisphere. The name America was thus directly attributed to Amerigo Vespucci.
title: Early world maps

text: Located at the intersection of Texas and Oklahoma, Texhoma stands as a unique town straddling the state line, with the Texas–Oklahoma border dividing it into two separate parts: Texhoma, Oklahoma, and Texhoma, Texas. This division reflects both the geographic and cultural blend of the two states, as the town's name is a portmanteau of Texas and Oklahoma. Situated in Texas County, Oklahoma, it was originally developed around the arrival of the Rock Island Railroad, and its economy remains rooted in ranching and livestock. The 2010 census recorded a population of 926.
title: Texhoma, Oklahoma

text: A key focus within sport psychology, particularly in the sub-field of performance enhancement, is arousal regulation. This involves entering into and maintaining an optimal level of cognitive and physiological activation in order to maximize performance. Techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, breathing exercises, and meditation are used to reduce anxiety when arousal is too high, while energizing methods like listening to music or using energizing cues help when alertness is low. The Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) Theory, formed in 2001, is a widely adopted form of mindfulness in sport and includes regular meditation and acceptance practices before and during competition. These protocols have been tested with NCAA men's and women's basketball players, and one study found that an NCAA women's basketball player increased her personal satisfaction in her performances from 2.4 out of 10 to 9.2 out of 10 after performing the specific MAC protocol for several weeks. Arousal regulation is thus central to performance enhancement in sport.
title: Sport psychology

text: Set in the 1920s, The Quiet Man follows Sean Thornton, an Irish-born American from Pittsburgh, as he travels to Ireland to reclaim his family's farm and his birthplace in Inisfree. The story unfolds during this era, highlighting the social dynamics and personal conflicts of the time.

text: Known as the cradle of civilization, Mesopotamia is recognized as the earliest region where human civilization emerged, based on current archaeological evidence. The Fertile Crescent, which includes Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt, is widely understood to be the first area to develop complex societies. Among these, Mesopotamia stands out as the oldest civilization known to man.
title: Cradle of civilization

text: The fertile crescent region, and Mesopotamia in particular, are often referred to as the cradle of civilization. Around 10,200 BC, the first fully developed Neolithic cultures, including the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B phases, emerged in this region and spread in various directions. In Mesopotamia, the convergence of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers created rich fertile soil and a reliable water supply for irrigation, enabling the development of some of the earliest known non-nomadic agrarian societies. The Ubaid period (c. 6500 to 3800 BC) marks the earliest known period on the alluvial plain, and it was during this time that urbanization began to take shape. Eridu is the oldest Sumerian site settled during this period, around 5300 BC, and the city of Ur also first dates to the end of this period. Because of these early developments, Mesopotamia is recognized as the oldest civilization known to man.
title: Cradle of civilization

text: Anatomy is the branch of science that deals with the structure of human body parts, and the term "anatomy" is commonly taken to refer to human anatomy. While similar structures and tissues are found in other animals, the field also encompasses the study of animal anatomy, with zootomy sometimes used to specifically refer to animals. The structure and tissues of plants, however, are fundamentally different and are studied in a separate discipline known as plant anatomy.
title: Anatomy

text: The branch of science that deals with the structure of human body parts is known as Anatomy. Human anatomy can be taught regionally or systemically; that is, respectively, studying anatomy by bodily regions such as the head and chest, or studying by specific systems, such as the nervous or respiratory systems. The major anatomy textbook, Gray's Anatomy, has been reorganized from a systems format to a regional format, in line with modern teaching methods. A thorough working knowledge of anatomy is required by physicians, especially surgeons and doctors working in some diagnostic specialties, such as histopathology and radiology.
title: Anatomy

text: The woolly mammoth, a large herbivore that thrived in the cold environments of the last ice age, primarily fed on grass and sedges. This diet supported its energy needs in the vast, open grasslands known as the mammoth steppe, which spanned across northern Eurasia and North America. With a body structure adapted to extreme cold—featuring thick fur, short ears, and a short tail—the woolly mammoth lived in conditions that favored such vegetation. Its behavior mirrored that of modern elephants, using its trunk and tusks for foraging, manipulation, and defense.
title: Woolly mammoth

text: Woolly mammoths sustained themselves on plant food, mainly grass and sedges, which were supplemented with herbaceous plants, flowering plants, shrubs, mosses, and tree matter. This dietary pattern is supported by findings of food at various stages of digestion in their intestines, offering a clear picture of what they consumed. The composition of their diet varied by location, but the primary components remained consistent. Like modern elephants, they required a diverse range of vegetation to support their large body size, with an adult weighing six tonnes needing to consume 180 kg (397 lb) daily and foraging up to twenty hours each day. Their two-fingered trunk tip was adapted to grasp the short grasses of the last ice age, and the trunk could also be used to pull grass tufts, pick buds and flowers, and tear leaves and branches from shrubs and trees. The "Yukagir mammoth" had ingested plant matter containing spores of dung fungus, and isotope analysis confirms that woolly mammoths fed mainly on C3 plants.
title: Woolly mammoth

text: The process of mitosis involves the division of one nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei. This process is divided into stages—prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase—each marking the completion of specific cellular activities. During mitosis, chromosomes, which have already duplicated, condense and attach to spindle fibers that pull one copy of each chromosome to opposite sides of the cell. The result is two genetically identical daughter nuclei. While the rest of the cell may divide through cytokinesis to form two daughter cells, errors such as tripolar or multipolar mitosis can lead to the production of three or more daughter cells. Such errors may also trigger apoptosis or cause mutations, potentially contributing to the development of certain cancers.
title: Mitosis

text: Star formation in the Milky Way today primarily happens within molecular clouds in interstellar space, often called "stellar nurseries" or "star-forming regions." These dense regions serve as the birthplaces where gravity causes material to collapse and eventually form stars. The process begins in giant molecular clouds (GMC), which are key components of the interstellar medium and act as precursors to star formation. As the material within these clouds condenses, it gives rise to protostars and young stellar objects, marking the progression from interstellar gas to fully formed stars.

text: The most recent technological change to the U.S. economy was the digitization of social systems. This shift marks the latest phase in a series of long waves of technological advancement, following earlier transformations driven by water-powered mechanization, steam power, electrification, motorization, and automation. According to the framework of Kondratiev waves, the current phase is defined by the widespread integration of digital technologies into social and economic structures, enabling unprecedented levels of productivity and reshaping societal organization. Digital Information and Communication Technologies fulfill the criteria of a general purpose technology—characterized by low and descending relative costs, unlimited supply, all-pervasiveness, and the ability to reduce costs across capital, labor, and products—thereby driving a fundamental transformation of the economy into a post-industrial, information-based society.
title: Digital Revolution

text: Itai-itai disease was a form of poisoning associated with ingestion of cadmium. This disease emerged in Toyama Prefecture as a result of cadmium poisoning from mining activities that began as early as 1710, with regular silver mining starting in 1589 and subsequent mining of lead, copper, and zinc. During periods of increased demand during the Russo-Japanese War and World War I, along with the introduction of European mining technologies, mining output surged, placing the Kamioka Mines among the world's top producers. Production expanded further before World War II, and starting in 1910 and continuing through 1945, cadmium was released in significant quantities by mining operations, leading to the first appearance of the disease around 1912. The mining, operated by Mitsui Mining & Smelting Co., Ltd., intensified to meet wartime needs, which in turn increased pollution of the Jinzū River and its tributaries—water sources used for irrigation, drinking, washing, fishing, and other daily activities by local populations.
title: Itai-itai disease

text: The Confederate States of America emerged from a deep-rooted regional identity, with many southern whites viewing themselves as more Southern than American and prepared to defend their states' independence from the Union. This regionalism evolved into a distinct Southern nationalism, known as the "Cause," which became the foundation of the Confederacy’s existence during the Civil War. The "Cause" was not merely rooted in states' rights or economic policies, but was fundamentally tied to the cultural and financial dependence on the South’s slavery-based economy. As historian John M. Coski noted, "The statesmen who led the secession movement were unashamed to explicitly cite the defense of slavery as their prime motive... Acknowledging the centrality of slavery to the Confederacy is essential for understanding the Confederate." Thus, the Confederacy stands as the entity that supported states' rights during the Civil War.
title: Confederate States of America

text: The cytoskeleton plays a vital role in cellular structure and function, with one of its key components being the microfilament. Microfilaments are composed of the most abundant cellular protein known as actin, highlighting their central role in cellular processes such as muscle contraction. In muscle cells, these actin filaments interact with myosin molecular motors to generate force during contraction, a process initiated by nerve impulses that trigger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increase in calcium allows tropomyosin to move away from the actin-binding sites, enabling actin and myosin to interact and initiate contraction. This dynamic interaction underscores the importance of microfilaments in maintaining cellular integrity and enabling movement.
title: Cytoskeleton

text:
The field that examines how brain structure and function influence behavior and mental processes is known as neuropsychology. This discipline bridges the gap between the nervous system and psychological functions, focusing specifically on how the brain contributes to cognition and behavior. Unlike traditional psychology, which often separates mental processes from biological factors, neuropsychology integrates neuroscience to explore the mind-body connection. It is especially concerned with understanding the effects of brain damage on behavior and is used in diagnosing and treating cognitive impairments linked to neurological conditions. The study includes both human and animal lesion research and involves recording neural activity in primates, including human patients. Neuropsychology draws on neuroscience and aligns with cognitive psychology in its view of the mind as a system that processes information.  

neuropsychology
title: Neuropsychology

text: Neuropsychology is the approach to psychology that focuses on the body, especially the brain and nervous system. Experimental neuropsychology uses methods from experimental psychology to explore the relationship between the nervous system and cognitive function, often studying healthy humans in laboratory settings. This field leverages specific features of the nervous system—such as how visual information from one side of the visual field is processed by the opposite cortical hemisphere—to establish connections between neuroanatomy and psychological processes. The discipline emphasizes understanding how brain structure and function influence behavior and cognition.
title: Neuropsychology
